questions.question: What two operations must a vector space be equipped with?
options: Vector addition and multiplication of two vectors.
Vector addition and scalar multiplication.
Scalar multiplication and the dot product.
Vector addition and a length for each vector.

questions.question: Why is $\mathbb{R}^n$ the standard example of a vector space?
options: It has coordinatewise addition and real scalar multiplication.
It has coordinatewise addition and coordinatewise multiplication.
Its vectors have lengths and angles, which define a vector space.
Every vector space is a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ for some $n$.

questions.question: Do the polynomials of degree at most $2$ form a vector space under the usual addition and scalar multiplication?
options: Yes
No; they have no zero element
No; they are not closed under addition
Only over $\mathbb{C}$

questions.question: Which vector-space axiom fails for $\{(x,y)\colon x+y=1\}$ under ordinary operations?
options: Addition on it is not commutative.
The scalar identity $1x=x$ fails on it.
It does not contain the zero vector.
It is a line, and no line can be a vector space.

questions.question: The set of all $m\times n$ real matrices is a vector space under which operations?
options: Matrix multiplication and real scalar multiplication.
Matrix addition and multiplication by other matrices.
Matrix addition and transposition, $A\mapsto A^{\top}$.
Matrix addition and real scalar multiplication.

questions.question: In a vector space, what is $0\cdot v$ (the zero scalar times any vector $v$)?
options: The zero vector $\boldsymbol0$
The vector $v$ itself
The real number $0$
Undefined unless $v=\boldsymbol0$

questions.question: What does the cancellation law say in a vector space?
options: If $x+y=x+z$, then $y=z$.
If $xy=xz$, then $y=z$.
If $x+y=x+z$, then $x=z$.
If $\alpha x=\alpha y$, then $x=y$.

questions.question: Which statement uses distributivity over vector addition?
options: $\alpha(x+y)=\alpha x+\alpha y$
$(\alpha+\beta)x=\alpha x+\beta x$
$\alpha(\beta x)=(\alpha\beta)x$

questions.question: Why is checking only closure under addition not enough to prove a set is a vector space?
options: Closure must also hold for multiplying two vectors together.
Closure under addition also gives closure under scalar multiplication.
Scalar closure, zero, inverses and the other axioms must hold too.
Only the zero vector must also be checked; the rest is automatic.

questions.question: If $u,v\in V$ and $\alpha,\beta$ are scalars, must $\alpha u+\beta v\in V$?
options: Yes, by closure.
Only if $\alpha+\beta=1$.
Only if $\alpha,\beta\ge0$.
Only if $u,v$ are independent.

questions.question: With the usual addition and scalar multiplication, is $\mathbb{R}^2$ a vector space over the field $\mathbb{C}$?
options: No: $\mathrm{i}(1,0)=(\mathrm{i},0)$ is not in $\mathbb{R}^2$, so scalar closure fails.
Yes: $\mathbb{R}\subseteq\mathbb{C}$, so every real vector space is also complex.
Yes: the addition axioms hold, and they do not depend on the field.
No: over $\mathbb{C}$ the space $\mathbb{R}^2$ has no zero vector.

questions.question: A set with an addition and a scalar multiplication contains the zero vector $\boldsymbol{0}$ and a vector $\boldsymbol{x}$, but no vector $\boldsymbol{y}$ with $\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{0}$. Which axiom is certainly violated?
options: Distributivity over vector addition
Commutativity of vector addition
Existence of an additive identity
Existence of additive inverses
